title: Loops
summary: A loop repeats steps. A for loop can visit each item in a list, one after another.
introduction: A loop repeats steps. A for loop can visit each item in a list, one after another. Imagine reading every name on a class list. Write the greeting step once, then let the loop use it for each name.
learningObjectives: Iterate over lists, strings and ranges with for
Repeat until a condition changes with while, and stop early with break
Skip iterations with continue and use enumerate() and zip() for indexes and pairs
Spot off-by-one errors in range() and infinite while loops

blocks.text: `for item in collection:` takes the items one at a time, in order, and runs the block once for each. The loop variable is just a name you choose; `fruit`, `letter` and `n` are ordinary variables that keep their last value after the loop ends. The bare `print()` after the letter loop ends the line that `end=" "` left open.

To repeat something a fixed number of times, or to count, loop over a `range`. `range(stop)` counts from `0` up to but not including `stop`; `range(start, stop)` and `range(start, stop, step)` let you choose where to start and how far to jump, including backwards with a negative step.

blocks.title: ranges.py
blocks.code:
for i in range(5):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

for i in range(10, 0, -3):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

print(list(range(0, 20, 5)))
print(sum(range(1, 101)))

blocks.text: The exclusive end is deliberate: `range(len(items))` produces exactly the valid indexes of `items`, and `range(a, b)` always has `b - a` numbers. A range is not a list but a lazy description of the numbers, which is why `range(1, 101)` costs almost nothing even for huge ranges; wrap it in `list()` when you need the actual items.

blocks.title: Off by one
blocks.text: `range(1, 10)` stops at 9. If you want the numbers 1 to 10 inclusive, write `range(1, 11)`. The same rule applies to slices: `items[0:3]` gives three items, at indexes 0, 1 and 2. When a loop runs one time too few or too many, check the end value first.

blocks.title: countdown.py
blocks.code:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count -= 1
print("Lift-off!")

number = 1
while True:
    number *= 2
    if number > 100:
        break
print("First power of two above 100:", number)

blocks.text: `while` re-tests its condition before every repetition and stops as soon as the condition is false. Something inside the loop must move towards that moment, here `count -= 1`, or the loop never ends. `while True:` with a `break` is the idiom for loops whose exit condition sits in the middle of the work, such as reading commands until the user types `quit`.

blocks.title: Infinite loops
blocks.text: Forget `count -= 1` and the condition stays true forever: the program hangs and the terminal shows nothing. Press Ctrl+C to stop it (Python raises `KeyboardInterrupt`), then make sure every `while` loop changes something its condition depends on, or contains a `break` that is guaranteed to be reached.

blocks.title: break_continue.py

blocks.text: `continue` jumps straight to the next iteration; `break` leaves the loop entirely. A `for` loop may also have an `else` block, which runs only when the loop finished *without* hitting `break`. That makes it a tidy way to express a search: the `else` is the "not found" case.

Two helpers remove most of the index arithmetic from loops. `enumerate()` yields `(index, item)` pairs, so you never have to write `range(len(items))` and index by hand; `zip()` walks two or more sequences in parallel and stops at the shortest.

blocks.text: A loop inside a loop runs the inner loop completely for every pass of the outer one. That is how you build tables and grids; the `:3` in the f-string right-aligns each number in a field three characters wide.

questions.explanation: `range(2, 11, 4)` starts at 2 and adds 4 each time while staying below 11: 2, 6, 10. The next value, 14, is out of range.
questions.code:
for i in range(2, 11, 4):
    print(i, end=" ")

questions.question: What does `continue` do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: `continue` abandons the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one; `break` is the statement that ends the loop entirely.
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one
Restarts the loop from the first item
Pauses the loop until the user presses a key
